name: Tris-biphenyl triazine

lead: Tris-biphenyl triazine is a synthetic UV filter sold as Tinosorb A2B. Skincare enthusiasts look for it in daily-wear sunscreens for broad coverage against the photoaging and pigmentation that sun exposure causes.

It is a particulate triazine-class filter that absorbs UVB and UVA and also scatters some light, described as a recent addition to the filters authorised in Europe. It has also been tested as a photostabilizer for avobenzone. Published work is laboratory and formulation research; no human trials of its effect on skin appearance were found.

paras: It is an ingredient in sunscreen formulations, typically combined with other filters in a daily facial SPF. Approval and permitted concentrations differ by country.
No compound-specific human safety trials were found. Approval and maximum concentrations vary by country, and UV filters as a class are the subject of ongoing safety and environmental assessment.

chain: Broad UV protection in daily wear
angle.text: Tris-biphenyl triazine (Tinosorb A2B) is a newer particulate filter that skincare enthusiasts look for in daily-wear sunscreens. It absorbs UVB and UVA and scatters some light, so protection against photoaging and pigmentation stays broad. Research so far is laboratory and formulation work.

lead: Tris-biphenyl triazine (TBPT), marketed as Tinosorb A2B, is a synthetic ultraviolet (UV) filter used in sunscreens and daily-wear skincare. It helps people look better over the long term by blocking the UV exposure that drives visible skin aging, uneven pigmentation and sunburn: a sunscreen that carries a strong, photostable filter lets users protect their skin on the face every day without the formula degrading in sunlight.[1][2]

TBPT is a particulate organic filter: it is made as a micronised, water-insoluble nanoparticle dispersion rather than a dissolved oil-soluble molecule. It belongs to the triazine family alongside bemotrizinol (Tinosorb S) and was introduced as the first filter added to Annex VI of the European Cosmetics Regulation after that regulation took effect in July 2013.[3][3] A review by one of the chemists involved in developing the Tinosorb filters describes it as having the highest efficacy of all cosmetic UV absorbers on the market when measured by area under the UV spectrum.[1]

Published work on the filter consists mainly of formulation, optical and photochemical studies, plus its use as a photostabiliser for other filters such as avobenzone.[4][5][6] No clinical trials of its effects on skin appearance have been published, and in looksmaxxing circles it appears only as one ingredient in sunscreen formulations.

paras: Tris-biphenyl triazine is a large, water-insoluble organic molecule with a triazine core carrying three biphenyl groups. Because it does not dissolve in water or most cosmetic oils well, it is prepared as an aqueous dispersion of nanoparticles made of the absorber molecules themselves; these particles show strong UV absorbance.[2][2]

The 2016 review describing its development presents TBPT as the product of a concept of micronised organic UV absorbers, developed alongside the oil-soluble filter bemotrizinol (BEMT, Tinosorb S). In that account BEMT is widely used in both beach and skincare products, while TBPT was introduced as a UV filter with the highest efficacy per the area under the UV spectrum.[1]

Photophysical work has examined why the particles absorb as they do. Quantum-chemical (DFT) calculations and spectra of dissolved versus dispersed material showed that the nanoparticle dispersion's spectrum differs slightly from the dissolved molecule, with an additional shoulder at longer wavelengths, which the authors explained by pi-stacked aggregates of TBPT molecules.[2]

A 2015 paper in the International Journal of Pharmaceutics describes TBPT as a filter that helps formulators meet the European recommendation for broad-spectrum protection, a critical wavelength of at least 370 nm, in a market with few authorised filters.[3] The same paper reports that each percent of TBPT in a formula contributed roughly 2 SPF units and 1 UVA-PF unit, and that SPF and UVA-PF did not change after two hours of irradiation in a solar simulator, which the authors cite as evidence of high photostability.[3]

Unlike dissolved filters that only absorb, particulate filters can also scatter light. A 2025 study in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science used TBPT as its example and set out to measure how much of its protection comes from scattering, including forward and backward scattering, reporting that the effectiveness of TBPT is associated with both absorption and scattering.[6]

TBPT is commonly paired with avobenzone, a UVA filter that is itself unstable in sunlight. A 2021 laboratory study evaluated TBPT as one of three avobenzone photostabilisers (with ethylhexyl methoxycrylene and a citrate-based stabiliser) in formulations also containing retinyl palmitate and octyl methoxycinnamate. All three improved the photostability of avobenzone and retinyl palmitate in UVA exposure, while ethylhexyl methoxycrylene was the most effective at stabilising retinyl palmitate and at reducing phototoxicity in a 3T3 cell assay.[4]

A 2026 paper reports a validated HPLC method for measuring avobenzone and TBPT simultaneously, noting that the combination enables broad-spectrum photoprotection and improved photostability and that both compounds are highly hydrophobic and hard to analyse in complex formulations.[5]

Wikipedia notes that sunscreen filters in general are described in terms of the spectrum they cover, and lists TBPT among filters offering both UVA and UVB protection.[7] Bemotrizinol's Wikipedia entry likewise lists synergistic SPF effects with other triazine and benzotriazole filters, a pairing logic that also applies to how formulators combine TBPT with other filters.[8]

Approval and maximum permitted concentrations vary by jurisdiction.[7] In the EU, TBPT was the first filter registered in Annex VI of Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 after the regulation came into force in July 2013.[3] A 2020 review about designing new sunscreen agents notes that currently used UV filters as a class have limitations that researchers cite, including systemic absorption, endocrine disruption, allergy and cytotoxicity concerns; it refers to filters as a class, not TBPT specifically.[9]

Recent computational and environmental work treats UV filters as a group: a 2026 study used molecular dynamics to examine how organic UV filters bind human transporter proteins relevant to skin absorption and toxicity, and another 2026 paper proposed non-animal methods to screen cosmetic UV filters for persistence, bioaccumulation, toxicity and endocrine activity.[10][11] Large particulate filters such as TBPT are designed to remain on the skin surface rather than be absorbed, a property attributed to their size in descriptions of the micronised-filter concept.[1]

No studies found of TBPT's effects in human trials on skin appearance or photoaging. Published research is limited to laboratory, optical and formulation studies, including the in vitro and solar-simulator work described above.[3][4][6][2]

The compound is not the subject of its own community protocols. Skincare discussions that mention it treat it as an ingredient in broad-spectrum sunscreens, where proponents of sun protection for preventing skin aging may look for newer filters such as Tinosorb A2B and Tinosorb S on ingredient lists; this reflects general sunscreen discussion rather than claims specific to the compound.
